property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract only accepts fallback calls when msg.value == 10 ether and thus updates pastBlockTime (so after a successful call pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1); the mutant accepting msg.value >= 10 ether can allow extra calls (with >10 ether) that change whether pastBlockTime is updated under the same inputs, so there exist inputs where pastBlockTime differs between reference and mutant.

For every call to fallback() with any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract only proceeds and updates pastBlockTime when msg.value == 10 ether (so after a successful call pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1); the mutant that uses require(msg.value >= 10 ether) allows additional values (msg.value > 10 ether) to proceed and thus can make pastBlockTime differ, so the invariant "after a call completes, pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1 iff the call did not revert" holds for the reference for all inputs but is broken by the mutant for some inputs.

For any external call to fallback with any caller and any amount, the reference contract only accepts calls that send exactly 10 ether, and whenever the call succeeds the contract's public pastBlockTime becomes block.timestamp + 1; the mutant allowing msg.value >= 10 ether lets additional amounts (>10 ether) succeed and thus can make pastBlockTime differ — so the rule: after a fallback call completes successfully, pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1 (holds for reference for all inputs), which the mutant violates for some inputs.

For every successful call to fallback (i.e., the call does not revert), the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp + 1; the mutant accepting msg.value >= 10 ether can succeed on values != 10 ether and thereby allow a successful call that does not set pastBlockTime to block.timestamp + 1 under the same observable conditions, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any call to fallback with any caller and any value, the reference contract only proceeds when msg.value == 10 ether and when it succeeds it sets pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1; the mutant that accepts msg.value >= 10 ether allows calls with value > 10 ether to also succeed and thus can make pastBlockTime differ from block.timestamp + 1 for some inputs.

After any successful fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the stored pastBlockTime strictly increases beyond the previous stored value (reference sets pastBlockTime = block.timestamp + 1), but the mutant that sets pastBlockTime = block.timestamp can leave pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp allowing a non-strict increase (violating the strict-increase rule) for some inputs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from an EOA at a time strictly after the previous stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to a value > block.timestamp (i.e., block.timestamp+1) so after the call pastBlockTime != block.timestamp, whereas the mutant that assigns pastBlockTime = block.timestamp can make pastBlockTime == block.timestamp for some inputs, violating this rule.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference C always increases pastBlockTime to strictly greater than the previous value (i.e., preserves monotonic increase when invoked), whereas the mutant removing the require can allow pastBlockTime to be set to the same or a non-increasing value when block.timestamp does not advance (breaking monotonicity).

For any caller who sends exactly 10 ether to fallback at strictly increasing block.timestamp values, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to a strictly increasing value (each successful call makes pastBlockTime > previous), while the mutant (which removes the require enforcing timestamp > pastBlockTime) can allow pastBlockTime to stay non-increasing when calls happen at non-increasing timestamps, so monotonic increase of pastBlockTime across sequential fallback calls is guaranteed by the reference and can be violated by the mutant.

For any single call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference C either reverts if the supplied block.timestamp is not strictly greater than stored pastBlockTime, or if it succeeds then it sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp+1; the mutant (which removed the require) can succeed and set pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp <= prior pastBlockTime, so there exists an input (a call at non-increasing timestamp) where the mutant's pastBlockTime differs from the reference.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to fallback, the reference contract always reverts when the current block.timestamp is not strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime (so pastBlockTime only updates when timestamp advances), whereas the mutant (removing that require) can accept a call at a non-increasing timestamp and thus update pastBlockTime when the reference would have reverted.

For any single fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether, the reference contract either reverts if block.timestamp is not strictly greater than pastBlockTime, or (if it succeeds) sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp+1; the mutant can accept calls at non-increasing timestamps and thus allow a successful call that updates pastBlockTime when the reference would have reverted.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at a block whose timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime, the reference C only drains its balance when block.number % 15 == 0 (so address(c).balance remains nonzero for calls where block.number % 15 != 0); the mutant flips the condition and will sometimes drain on block numbers where %15 != 0, so observing address(c).balance after a call distinguishes them.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than pastBlockTime, the reference contract only empties its balance when block.number % 15 == 0, so for all admissible inputs if we pick a block number such that block.number % 15 != 0 then after the call address(c).balance remains nonzero (the mutant flips the condition and will drain on those blocks).

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether from a contract whose receive/fallback always succeeds, if the call is made at a block number that is a multiple of 15 then the reference C will drain its balance (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant flips the conditional and will NOT drain on those multiples of 15, so there exists inputs (a caller contract and block number multiple of 15) that make the mutant diverge.

For any caller and block timestamp where the call succeeds, the contract's pastBlockTime is set to exactly block.timestamp + 1 after the fallback completes; the mutant increments it an extra 1 so this rule is violated for inputs where the call succeeds.

For any successful payable call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract sets pastBlockTime to exactly block.timestamp + 1; the mutant sometimes sets it to a different value (one greater), violating that equality.

For any successful payable fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to exactly block.timestamp + 1; the mutant sometimes stores a larger value (an extra +1), violating that equality.

For any successful payable call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always leaves pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp + 1; the mutant sometimes leaves it greater (block.timestamp + 2) due to an extra increment.

For any successful payable call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp + 1; the mutant sometimes stores a larger value (block.timestamp + 2) due to an extra increment, so asserting that pastBlockTime == block.timestamp + 1 after the call is a universal property the reference satisfies and the mutant violates for some inputs.
